nameStory: Wavy Meadow-grass gets its name from the distinctive wavy or zigzag pattern of its flowering stems, which bend back and forth like a gentle S-curve. The 'meadow-grass' part comes from its preference for open grasslands and its membership in the Poa genus, commonly called meadow-grasses throughout the world.
description: Wavy Meadow-grass is a delicate perennial grass that forms small, loose tufts rather than dense mats. It typically grows 1-2 feet tall with slender stems that have a characteristic wavy or flexuous appearance. The plant produces airy, open flower clusters in early summer and has narrow, soft green leaves that feel smooth to the touch.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: The flowering stems have a distinctive wavy, zigzag pattern that flexes back and forth - run your finger along the stem to feel the gentle curves and bends

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Loose, open flower clusters (panicles) with delicate, papery spikelets that rustle softly in the breeze and often have a slightly purplish tinge

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow grass blades about 1/8 inch wide that feel smooth and soft between your fingers, with a fresh green color and no rough edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, loose tufts or clumps rather than spreading into dense carpets, giving it an airy, delicate appearance in the landscape

habitat: Look for Wavy Meadow-grass in open woodlands, forest clearings, and meadow edges where it enjoys partial shade to full sun. It prefers well-drained soils and is often found in areas that are neither too wet nor too dry, growing alongside other native grasses and wildflowers.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge early, forming fresh tufts of narrow leaves. The characteristic wavy stems begin to develop as the plant prepares for flowering.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in early to mid-summer with delicate, airy seed heads swaying on the distinctive zigzag stems. Seeds ripen by late summer.
seasonality.fall: The plant begins to turn golden-brown and the wavy stems become more prominent as other vegetation dies back around it.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems persist through winter, still showing the wavy pattern that makes identification possible even in the dormant season.

funFact: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** The wavy stems of this grass may help it flex with strong winds rather than breaking, acting like natural shock absorbers in open meadows where gusts can be fierce.
confusionNotes: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Most other meadow-grasses have straight stems, so the wavy, flexuous stems are usually enough to distinguish this species. However, young plants before flowering may look similar to other small Poa species until the characteristic wavy stems develop.
contextualKnowledge: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Wavy Meadow-grass is quite rare in New England with only 3 recorded observations, so if you think you've found it, take photos and consider reporting your sighting to local botanists or iNaturalist for verification.
compareHints: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Unlike the common Smooth Meadow-grass which has straight stems and spreads by runners, or Annual Meadow-grass which is much smaller and weedy, Wavy Meadow-grass has those unmistakable zigzag stems and grows in neat tufts. Canada bluegrass might seem similar but has flattened, blue-green leaves and completely straight, stiff stems.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike Kentucky Bluegrass (Smooth Meadow-grass) which spreads by underground runners and forms smooth lawns, Bulbous Bluegrass grows in distinct clumps and has those telltale swollen stem bases.
Among its meadow-grass relatives, smooth meadow-grass stands out for its completely smooth leaf sheaths and strong spreading habit through rhizomes.
Among its meadow-grass relatives, Annual Meadow-grass is the softest to touch and stays the brightest green in cool weather.
Among the bluegrasses, Canada bluegrass is the only one with truly flattened stems - all its relatives like Kentucky bluegrass and annual bluegrass have round stems.
Compared to its Poa relatives like Kentucky Bluegrass and Annual Meadow-grass, Grove Meadow Grass is much more shade-tolerant and forms looser clumps rather than dense turf.
Among its Poa relatives, Wood Meadow-grass is distinguished by its shade tolerance and late-season growth habit.

Among its Poa relatives, Swamp Meadow-grass is the wetland specialist – while Smooth Meadow-grass (Kentucky bluegrass) prefers well-drained lawns and fields, and Canada bluegrass tolerates dry conditions, Swamp Meadow-grass needs consistently moist soil.

Unlike the common smooth meadow-grass (Kentucky bluegrass) that forms dense lawns, or the weedy annual meadow-grass found in sidewalk cracks, drooping bluegrass stays in small clumps and has that characteristic drooping flower display.
Among the meadow-grasses (Poa species), rough meadow-grass is the only one with consistently rough-textured stems and leaf sheaths.
Among New England's bluegrasses, glaucous bluegrass stands out for its waxy blue-gray coating and extreme habitat preferences.
